subject: Physics
axis_note: ladder_position is a curriculum coordinate. It is never a learner estimate, and Core1A/Core1B may not consult one.

rungs.aha: Angles in specular reflection are measured from the surface normal, and the reflected ray leaves with the same angle to that normal as the incident ray.
learner_owns: Can trace a directed straight path and identify where it meets a surface.
must_contain: The surface normal drawn at the point of incidence.
Both incident and reflected rays labeled before angles are compared.

misconception.wrong_idea: The angle of incidence is measured from the mirror surface.
misconception.diagnostic_prompt: A ray makes 20 degrees with the mirror surface. Is its angle of incidence 20 degrees?
misconception.repair: Draw the normal first; incidence and reflection angles are defined from that line, not from the surface.

rungs.closure: Given an incident ray and mirror surface, draw the normal and construct the reflected ray with equal normal-referenced angles.

controlled_variation.hold: the same plane mirror and point of incidence
controlled_variation.notice: the reflected ray changes so the two normal-referenced angles remain equal

controlled_variation.vary: the drawing orientation of the mirror
controlled_variation.hold: the physical incident and reflected geometry
controlled_variation.notice: rotating the page does not change the normal-based law

rungs.aha: An image location is determined by where reflected rays actually meet or where their backward extensions appear to meet; virtual describes ray geometry, not whether a camera can record it.
learner_owns: R1: reflection direction is fixed by equal angles measured from the normal.
must_contain: At least two reflected rays from one object point.
Solid rays for physical light paths and clearly distinguished backward extensions.

misconception.wrong_idea: A virtual image is not a usable image and therefore cannot be photographed.
misconception.diagnostic_prompt: A camera points at a plane mirror and records your reflection. Does that make the mirror image real?
misconception.repair: Separate image geometry from recording: the mirror sends diverging rays that a camera lens can collect and refocus.

rungs.closure: From a two-ray construction, classify an image as real or virtual from ray-intersection geometry and explain why either can be viewed.

controlled_variation.vary: observer or camera position within the reflected ray bundle
controlled_variation.hold: the same object and plane mirror
controlled_variation.notice: the virtual image location stays fixed even though different reflected rays reach the observer

controlled_variation.vary: whether rays actually converge or only backward extensions converge
controlled_variation.hold: the same rule for locating an image point
controlled_variation.notice: real versus virtual is decided by ray geometry, not by visibility

rungs.aha: The Cartesian sign convention turns a mirror diagram into signed distances and heights; the signs come from declared directions, not from memorized object/image labels.
learner_owns: R2: image nature is determined by actual versus backward-extended ray intersection.
must_contain: The pole, principal axis, and incident-light direction declared before distances receive signs.
One horizontal and one vertical sign decision shown explicitly.

misconception.wrong_idea: Object distance is always negative and image distance is always positive.
misconception.diagnostic_prompt: Move the same object-and-mirror sketch so incident light travels the opposite page direction. Should the sign rule follow the page or the declared incident-light direction?
misconception.repair: Apply the coordinate convention from the pole every time; signs follow measurement direction and height orientation.

rungs.closure: Assign signs to u, v, f, and image height on a stated mirror diagram without using a memorized object/image sign table.

controlled_variation.vary: whether a point lies with or against the incident-light direction
controlled_variation.hold: the pole and declared incident-light direction
controlled_variation.notice: distance sign follows direction from the pole

controlled_variation.vary: whether a point lies above or below the principal axis
controlled_variation.hold: the same axis and vertical-positive convention
controlled_variation.notice: height sign is independent of longitudinal distance sign

rungs.aha: Principal rays are construction shortcuts tied to spherical-mirror geometry, and a consistent pair of rays locates the image without requiring every ray to be drawn.
learner_owns: R3: signed optical coordinates are assigned from a declared pole, axis, and incident-light direction.
must_contain: Parallel-to-axis, through-focus, and through-center ray rules stated as paired before/after directions.
Two-ray intersections for multiple object positions.

misconception.wrong_idea: A principal ray diagram is a decorative sketch, so the ray rules can be mixed without affecting image location.
misconception.diagnostic_prompt: If two correctly constructed principal rays predict different image points, what must be wrong?
misconception.repair: Each principal ray is constrained by the same mirror geometry; use any valid pair and require a common intersection or common backward intersection.

rungs.closure: Construct an image with two principal rays and use a third principal ray as a consistency check.

controlled_variation.vary: which valid pair of principal rays is used
controlled_variation.hold: the same object point and mirror geometry
controlled_variation.notice: every valid pair locates the same image point

controlled_variation.vary: object position relative to focus and center of curvature
controlled_variation.hold: the same mirror and principal-ray rules
controlled_variation.notice: image position, orientation, and real/virtual character change systematically

rungs.aha: The spherical-mirror equation relates signed object distance, image distance, and focal length under the paraxial approximation; it is an algebraic model of the same geometry as the ray construction.
learner_owns: R4: a consistent principal-ray pair locates one image point for a stated spherical mirror.
must_contain: Signed u, v, and f inserted only after the diagram establishes the coordinate directions.
A ray-diagram estimate compared with the equation result.

misconception.wrong_idea: The mirror formula is exact for any ray striking any part of a spherical mirror.
misconception.diagnostic_prompt: Two rays strike far from the principal axis at large angles. Is the paraxial mirror formula guaranteed to predict their exact intersection?
misconception.repair: State the paraxial condition before using the formula and treat large-angle disagreement as a model-limit issue, not an algebra error.

rungs.closure: Given u and f with a declared sign convention, solve for v, classify the image, and state the paraxial condition behind the calculation.

controlled_variation.vary: object distance within the paraxial regime
controlled_variation.hold: mirror focal length and sign convention
controlled_variation.notice: the equation's predicted image location tracks the ray construction

controlled_variation.vary: ray height and angle away from the principal axis
controlled_variation.hold: the same spherical mirror and object
controlled_variation.notice: the simple formula becomes an approximation whose geometric agreement can degrade

rungs.aha: Magnification links image size and orientation to signed image/object distances; its sign carries orientation information rather than being an expendable algebraic detail.
learner_owns: R5: the mirror equation gives a signed image distance under a declared convention and paraxial model.
must_contain: Both ratios m = h_i/h_o and m = -v/u connected for the same image.
One case with negative magnification and one with positive magnification.

misconception.wrong_idea: Magnification is only the positive size ratio, so its sign can be discarded.
misconception.diagnostic_prompt: Two images are equally large, one erect and one inverted. Can one unsigned magnification value distinguish them?
misconception.repair: Keep the sign: magnitude tells relative size while sign records erect versus inverted orientation under the convention.

rungs.closure: Use signed u and v to compute magnification, then predict image orientation and relative size before checking against a ray diagram.

controlled_variation.vary: object position for one concave mirror
controlled_variation.notice: magnification magnitude and sign change as image position and orientation change

controlled_variation.vary: how much of the mirror aperture is uncovered
controlled_variation.hold: object position and the remaining mirror curvature
controlled_variation.notice: image brightness changes while the whole geometric image and magnification remain

family.invariant_demand: Translate the mirror geometry into a reflected-ray construction and signed optical quantities, determine image position and nature, and cross-check size and orientation with magnification.
family.difficult_move: Keeping the geometric ray picture and the Cartesian sign convention consistent before substituting into formulas.
family.independent_check: A valid ray construction, the signed mirror equation, and the magnification sign must predict compatible image location and orientation.

support_ladder.handed_over: The normal or principal rays are started, the pole/axis are labeled, and the incident-light direction for signs is declared.
The mirror, object, pole, and principal axis are labeled, but the learner chooses rays and signs.
Only the physical mirror setup and requested image quantity are supplied.

transfer.changed_demand: Use a wide-aperture spherical mirror with rays far from the principal axis and decide whether the paraxial mirror model is adequate.
transfer.information_not_handed_over: whether the small-angle/paraxial condition is satisfied

transfer.changed_demand: Convert between a ray diagram and signed u, v, f, and magnification values without changing the physical prediction.
transfer.information_not_handed_over: the sign assignments implied by the incident-light and height directions

transfer.changed_demand: Predict what happens to the image when half of a concave mirror is covered.
transfer.information_not_handed_over: that each object point sends usable rays to many parts of the mirror so aperture affects brightness rather than image completeness

transfer.changed_demand: A camera photographs a plane-mirror image; trace the mirror's virtual image as the object presented to the camera lens.
transfer.information_not_handed_over: the intermediate virtual-image location defined by backward extensions of reflected rays
